blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Logistics KPIs only work in practice if three conditions are met: the numbers are trusted, the review cadence is regular, and the meeting actually produces decisions. A beautiful dashboard that nobody believes, or that gets looked at only in a crisis, is worse than useless — it gives the illusion of control without the discipline.

Good teams are ruthless about data hygiene. They fix calculation errors the day they appear. They agree, in writing, what each KPI measures and what it excludes. And they review the small core — on-time delivery, cost per shipment, damage rate, customer complaint rate — at the same time every week, with the same small group, making the same small number of decisions.

Over a year, this unglamorous rhythm produces the kind of operational stability that looks easy from the outside. It is not. It is the patient accumulation of a very disciplined weekly hour.

items.q: According to the text, which three conditions must be met for logistics KPIs to work?
options: Daily reviews, external auditors, and long reports
New metrics, more meetings, and detailed forecasts
A large dashboard, expensive software, and a big team
Trusted numbers, a regular cadence, and decisions from the meeting
items.why: "the numbers are trusted, the review cadence is regular, and the meeting actually produces decisions."

items.q: Why does the author call an unbelieved dashboard "worse than useless"?
options: It gives the illusion of control without the discipline
It takes too long to update each week
It costs too much to build and maintain
items.why: "it gives the illusion of control without the discipline."

items.q: What does the text mean by teams being "ruthless about data hygiene"?
options: They delete metrics that look bad
They report only to the ops director
They fix calculation errors the day they appear and define each KPI in writing
They review every metric available, not just a core set
items.why: "They fix calculation errors the day they appear. They agree, in writing, what each KPI measures and what it excludes."

items.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
options: Defining what a KPI excludes is as important as what it measures
The best dashboards are the ones that look the most impressive
A weekly review with the same small group builds discipline
Operational stability is harder to achieve than it appears
items.why: Inferência: o texto trata um dashboard bonito e não confiável como pior que inútil — aparência não é o critério.

items.q: What does "It is not" (about the rhythm looking easy) suggest?
options: Outsiders understand the process better than insiders
Logistics KPIs rarely produce any stability
The weekly meeting should be replaced by daily ones
Stability comes from sustained, disciplined effort, not luck
items.why: Inferência: o que parece fácil de fora é, na verdade, o acúmulo paciente de uma hora semana disciplinada.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Harry explicando como está reconstruindo o dashboard. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Right, let me be honest about where we are. Two of our metrics were calculated inconsistently for three months. The ops director spotted it before we did, and that has cost us credibility we now have to earn back.

So I'm rebuilding the dashboard from the ground up. First, I've written a one-line definition for every KPI — what it measures, and just as importantly, what it excludes. On-time delivery, for example, now clearly excludes shipments the customer rescheduled. No more arguing in the meeting about whether a number is real.

Second, we're shrinking the review to a small core: on-time delivery, cost per shipment, damage rate, complaint rate. Same four numbers, same half hour every Tuesday, same three people. If a figure looks wrong, we fix the calculation that day — we don't wait for the next cycle.

And the rule I care about most: every review ends with at least one decision. If we look at the numbers and change nothing, we've wasted the hour. A dashboard nobody acts on is just decoration.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: Why does Harry say the team has to earn back credibility?
options: The dashboard was too slow to load
The ops director changed the KPI targets
The team missed several weekly reviews
Two metrics were calculated inconsistently and the ops director caught it first
items.why: "Two of our metrics were calculated inconsistently for three months. The ops director spotted it before we did."

items.q: What is the first thing Harry did when rebuilding the dashboard?
options: Wrote a one-line definition for every KPI, including what it excludes
Moved the meeting to a different day
Added more metrics to the review
items.why: "I've written a one-line definition for every KPI — what it measures, and just as importantly, what it excludes."

items.q: How does Harry describe the new review cadence?
options: An open meeting with no fixed agenda
Four core numbers, same half hour every Tuesday, same three people
A monthly deep-dive with the ops director
All metrics, reviewed daily by the whole team
items.why: "a small core… Same four numbers, same half hour every Tuesday, same three people."

items.q: What does Harry mean when he says "a dashboard nobody acts on is just decoration"?
options: The dashboard should be shown to more people
Metrics only matter if they lead to decisions
Decoration helps the team stay motivated
items.why: Inferência: sem uma decisão, o número não muda nada — o valor está na ação, não na tela.

items.q: What can we infer about Harry's approach to a figure that looks wrong?
options: He escalates it directly to the ops director
He treats it as urgent and fixes the calculation the same day
He removes the metric from the dashboard
He waits for the next cycle to review it calmly
items.why: Inferência: "If a figure looks wrong, we fix the calculation that day — we don't wait for the next cycle."

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "We review the same metrics on a weekly cadence." A cadence is…
items.why: Cadence = cadência: o ritmo regular e repetido da revisão.

items.q: "Good teams are ruthless about data hygiene." Ruthless here means…
items.why: Ruthless = implacável: rígido, sem tolerância com erros de dados.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "A dashboard nobody trusts gives the ___ of control, not the reality."
items.why: Illusion = ilusão: a falsa impressão de controle.

items.q: "We agreed in writing what each KPI measures and what it must exclude." To exclude means to…
items.why: To exclude = excluir: deixar de fora do cálculo.

items.q: "Stability is the patient accumulation of a disciplined weekly hour." Accumulation is…
items.why: Accumulation = acumulação: o resultado que se constrói pouco a pouco, semana após semana.

blocks.instruction: Expressões e phrasal verbs que aparecem em reuniões de KPIs e operações. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "The ops director still has to sign off on the new KPI definitions." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval final.

items.q: "We'll roll out the rebuilt dashboard to all regions next quarter." To roll out means to…
items.why: Roll out = implementar de forma progressiva.

items.q: "Fixing data hygiene will really move the needle on our credibility." This means it will…
items.why: Move the needle = mexer o ponteiro, fazer diferença perceptível.

items.q: "The team agreed the metric but never followed through on the fix." They…
options: failed to carry it to completion
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi combinado.

items.q: "When the on-time figure looked wrong, two analysts pushed back on the calculation." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, questionar, discordar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.
